source: The Doppler Effect
A source moving toward you sounds higher and one moving away sounds lower: f′ = f·v/(v ∓ vₛ).
Students think the pitch keeps rising as an approaching source gets closer, when it stays steady and then drops as the source passes.

An ambulance siren sounds higher as it comes toward you and lower as it goes away. The siren never changes; the waves reaching you do. The speed of sound is set by the air (What Sets a Wave's Speed), so motion changes the spacing of the crests you receive. As in Sound: Pitch and Loudness, the frequency you hear is the pitch.

$$f' = f\,\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$$ Use the upper signs when source and observer move toward each other, the lower signs when they move apart. Here $v$ is the speed of sound, $v_o$ the observer's speed and $v_s$ the source's. Approaching raises the pitch.
A moving source. Crests bunch up ahead and spread out behind, so the observer ahead hears a higher pitch.

A source with frequency $f$ sends a crest every $T = 1/f$. If it moves toward you at $v_s$, each crest starts $v_sT$ closer than the one before, so the crests arrive $\lambda' = (v - v_s)T$ apart. They still move at $v$, so you hear $f' = \frac{v}{\lambda'} = f\frac{v}{v - v_s}$. A moving observer meets crests more often: $f' = f\frac{v + v_o}{v}$.

Thinking the pitch keeps rising as an approaching source gets closer. At constant speed the higher pitch is steady; it drops suddenly to a lower steady pitch as the source passes you. Check with the formula: nothing in it depends on the distance.
A $600\ \text{Hz}$ siren moves at $30\ \text{m/s}$. What do you hear as it approaches and as it moves away? ($v = 343\ \text{m/s}$.)
An ambulance
$658\ \text{Hz}$, then $552\ \text{Hz}$
Approaching (upper sign in the denominator): $$f' = 600\,\dfrac{343}{343 - 30} = 600(1.096) = 658\ \text{Hz}.$$
Higher while approaching, lower after it passes.
You drive at $25\ \text{m/s}$ toward a factory whistle of $500\ \text{Hz}$ that stands still. What do you hear?
A moving listener
$536\ \text{Hz}$
Moving toward the source: $f' = f\,\dfrac{v + v_o}{v} = 500\,\dfrac{343 + 25}{343}$.
A train whistle of $400\ \text{Hz}$ sounds like $420\ \text{Hz}$ as the train approaches. How fast is the train?
Measuring a speed
About $16\ \text{m/s}$
Light does the same. Light from a galaxy moving away arrives with longer wavelengths (redshift), which is how astronomers measure the motions of stars and galaxies.
